warmup.q: A test app has 300 classes of its own. How many classes does the JVM load to run it to the end?
options: About 600: your classes plus the JDK classes they import
warmup.why: A generated 300-class app loaded 1,537 classes on JDK 21 with class sharing off: 301 from the app's JAR, 911 from the JDK's modules, and 325 hidden classes for lambdas and method handles. The JDK and the run-time machinery are most of the work, not your code. Your 300 classes are about a fifth of the total.

sections.h: Start-up is work the JVM repeats on every launch
sections.html:
A generated test app with 300 classes loads 1,537 classes on JDK 21 before it finishes, with class sharing turned off. 301 come from the app's JAR. 911 come from the JDK's own modules. The other 325 are hidden classes that the JVM spins up at run time for lambdas and method handles. Your 300 classes are a fifth of the work.

For every one of those classes the JVM does the same steps on every launch. It finds the bytes, parses them into its internal form in metaspace, verifies the bytecode, and later runs the static initializer. Then it runs your code in the interpreter, because the JIT compilers only start once they have profiles of what is hot. A framework adds its own start-up work on top: scanning the classpath for annotations, wiring beans by reflection, generating proxies, parsing config. Quarkus moves as much of that as it can to build time; its extension guide says to favor "doing work at build time ... as opposed to let the framework do work at startup time".

Nothing of this survives the process. Stop the JVM and the next start does it all again. Only one thing is cached by default: the JDK ships a class data sharing archive with about 1,300 of its own classes, which the JVM maps from disk instead of parsing. Lesson 2 of this track is about that archive and the bigger ones you can build.

You can watch the loading happen. -Xlog:class+load prints one line per class, and the end of each line says where the class came from:

[info][class,load] java.lang.Object source: shared objects file
[info][class,load] java.util.regex.Pattern$Node source: jrt:/java.base
[info][class,load] com.acme.pay.Main source: file:/srv/app.jar
[info][class,load] com.acme.pay.Main$$Lambda/0x... source: com.acme.pay.Main

shared objects file means the class was mapped from a CDS archive. jrt:/ means it was read and parsed from the JDK's modules file. file: is your classpath. A class name as the source marks a hidden class that this class defined at run time, usually a lambda. -verbose:class prints the same lines.

That source: column turns "start-up is slow" into a histogram you can read. When you try lesson 2's archives later, the same histogram shows them working.

try.title: Count where your classes come from
steps: Read ClassSourcesDemo. It starts a second JVM with -Xlog:class+load, runs a little start-up work there (regex, java.time, a stream, String.format), and groups the log lines by source:.
Predict: out of roughly 700 classes, how many come from the CDS archive? Then run it with the command below.
Run it again with -Pargs=-Xshare:off added. This turns the archive off for the child JVM.
Run the Kotlin twin (ClassSourcesDemoKt) once. Look at the file: line.

code.title: ClassSourcesDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l01.demo; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.LocalDate; import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.regex.Pattern; import java.util.stream.Collectors; /** * Starts a second JVM with -Xlog:class+load, runs a little start-up work in it, and counts * where each loaded class came from. Extra arguments are passed to that JVM as flags. */ public class ClassSourcesDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("--work")) { work(); return; } List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(List.of(args)); // e.g. -Xshare:off cmd.addAll(List.of("-Xlog:class+load", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), ClassSourcesDemo.class.getName(), "--work")); Process child = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); Map<String, Integer> bySource = new TreeMap<>(); try (var lines = child.inputReader().lines()) { lines.filter(l -> l.contains(" source: ")) .forEach(l -> bySource.merge(bucket(l), 1, Integer::sum)); } child.waitFor(); int total = bySource.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum(); System.out.printf("JDK %s, flags %s: %,d classes loaded%n", Runtime.version(), List.of(args), total); bySource.forEach((source, n) -> System.out.printf("%7d %s%n", n, source)); } /** Groups the "source:" field of a class+load line into a few buckets. */ static String bucket(String line) { String source = line.substring(line.indexOf(" source: ") + 9); if (source.equals("shared objects file")) return "shared objects file (the CDS archive)"; if (source.startsWith("jrt:/")) return "jrt:/ (the JDK's modules file, parsed now)"; if (source.startsWith("file:")) return "file: (your classes and JARs)"; return "other (hidden classes: lambdas, method handles)"; } /** A small taste of what services do at start-up: config, regex, dates, streams, lambdas. */ static void work() { Map<String, String> config = new TreeMap<>(); Pattern line = Pattern.compile("(\\w+(?:\\.\\w+)*)\\s*=\\s*(.*)"); for (String l : List.of("issuer.url = https://issuer.example", "pool.size = 20", "timeout.ms = 120")) { var m = line.matcher(l); if (m.matches()) config.put(m.group(1), m.group(2)); } String today = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 15).format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE); String summary = config.entrySet().stream() .map(e -> String.format("%s=%s", e.getKey(), e.getValue())) .collect(Collectors.joining(", ")); if (summary.isEmpty() || today.isEmpty()) throw new AssertionError(); } }

alt.title: ClassSourcesDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.startup.l01.demo import java.nio.file.Path import java.time.LocalDate import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter import java.util.TreeMap /** * Starts a second JVM with -Xlog:class+load, runs a little start-up work in it, and counts * where each loaded class came from. Extra arguments are passed to that JVM as flags. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "--work") { work() return } val cmd = buildList { add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()) addAll(args) // e.g. -Xshare:off addAll(listOf("-Xlog:class+load", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemoKt", "--work")) } val child = ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start() val bySource = TreeMap<String, Int>() child.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { " source: " in it }.forEach { bySource.merge(bucket(it), 1, Int::plus) } } child.waitFor() println("JDK ${Runtime.version()}, flags ${args.toList()}: %,d classes loaded".format(bySource.values.sum())) bySource.forEach { (source, n) -> println("%7d %s".format(n, source)) } } /** Groups the "source:" field of a class+load line into a few buckets. */ private fun bucket(line: String): String { val source = line.substringAfter(" source: ") return when { source == "shared objects file" -> "shared objects file (the CDS archive)" source.startsWith("jrt:/") -> "jrt:/ (the JDK's modules file, parsed now)" source.startsWith("file:") -> "file: (your classes and JARs, kotlin-stdlib too)" else -> "other (hidden classes: lambdas, method handles)" } } /** A small taste of what services do at start-up: config, regex, dates, collections, lambdas. */ private fun work() { val line = Regex("""(\w+(?:\.\w+)*)\s*=\s*(.*)""") val config = listOf("issuer.url = https://issuer.example", "pool.size = 20", "timeout.ms = 120") .mapNotNull { line.matchEntire(it)?.destructured } .associate { (key, value) -> key to value } .toSortedMap() val today = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 15).format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE) val summary = config.entries.joinToString(", ") { (k, v) -> "%s=%s".format(k, v) } check(summary.isNotEmpty() && today.isNotEmpty()) }

try.expect: On JDK 21 on a shared Linux VM: 734 classes, 718 from the shared objects file, 8 from jrt:/, 7 hidden, and 1 from file: (the demo itself). With -Xshare:off: 767 classes, 747 parsed from jrt:/, 19 hidden, none shared. JDK 25.0.4 loaded 818 with 793 shared, and 831 with sharing off. The Kotlin twin loads 876, with 63 from file:, because the Kotlin standard library is a JAR on your classpath like any other.

sections.h: Loading is lazy, and initialization is lazier
sections.html:
Loading a class and initializing it are two different events. The JVM loads a class when something needs its definition. It runs the class's static initializer, the method the bytecode calls <clinit>, only on the first active use: new, a call to a static method, a read or write of a static field that is not a compile-time constant, or a reflective call that asks for initialization. Initializing a subclass initializes its superclass first. Declaring a variable of the type does not initialize the class. Neither does Fees.class, which loads the class but runs no initializer.

That rule decides what ends up on your start-up path. Here is a common shape: a table built in a static field.

Java
public final class BinTable {
    private static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build();   // runs in <clinit>

    public static String version() { return "bins-2026.11"; }
    public static String issuerOf(String pan) { return TABLE.get(pan.substring(0, 6)); }
}
Kotlin
class BinTable {
    companion object {
        private val table = build()             // also runs in BinTable's <clinit>

        fun version() = "bins-2026.11"
        fun issuerOf(pan: String) = table[pan.take(6)]
    }
}

The readiness check only logs version(). It still pays for the whole table, because calling any static method initializes the class, and the class's initializer builds the table. The Kotlin version has the same problem, and it surprises people. A companion object's properties compile to static fields of the outer class, and the outer class's <clinit> fills them. javap -p lists table as a private static final field of BinTable itself.

The fix is the holder idiom: give the expensive field its own class.

Java
public final class BinTable {
    private static final class Holder {
        static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build();   // runs on first use of Holder
    }
    public static String version() { return "bins-2026.11"; }
    public static String issuerOf(String pan) { return Holder.TABLE.get(pan.substring(0, 6)); }
}
Kotlin
object BinTable {
    fun version() = "bins-2026.11"
    fun issuerOf(pan: String) = Holder.table[pan.take(6)]

    private object Holder {
        val table = build()                     // a nested object is its own class
    }
}

Now version() touches only BinTable. The JVM loads and initializes Holder the first time issuerOf reads Holder.TABLE. It is also thread-safe without any lock in your code: the JVM initializes a class under its own lock (JLS 12.4.2), so if eight threads arrive at once, one runs the initializer and the others wait for it. In Kotlin, val table by lazy { build() } gives you the same laziness with a lock you can see. Lesson 5 of the memory model track, "Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders", shows why this is safe.

Lazy is not always better. Moving the cost to the first request makes that request slow instead. Be lazy about work that many starts never need, such as admin tables or rarely used reports. Do the work early, on purpose, when every request needs it.

try.title: Predict the order of static initializers
steps: Write down the order of the log lines before you run it. Which line appears twice?
Run it. Then run the Kotlin twin, InitOrderDemoKt, which compares a companion object, a nested object and by lazy.

code.title: InitOrderDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Prints the moment each static initializer runs. Predict the order before you run it. */ public class InitOrderDemo { static final List<String> LOG = new ArrayList<>(); static Map<String, String> build(String who) { LOG.add(who); // the expensive part would go here return new HashMap<>(Map.of("411111", "Northwind Bank")); } /** The table is a static field of the class itself: built on first use of Eager. */ static class Eager { static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build("Eager.<clinit> builds the table"); static String version() { return "eager-v1"; } static Map<String, String> table() { return TABLE; } } /** The table lives in a nested holder: built on first use of Holder. */ static class Lazy { static { LOG.add("Lazy.<clinit> (no table here)"); } static String version() { return "lazy-v1"; } static Map<String, String> table() { return Holder.TABLE; } private static class Holder { static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build("Lazy.Holder.<clinit> builds the table"); } } public static void main(String[] args) { LOG.add("main starts"); Eager.version(); Lazy.version(); LOG.add("-- both versions read --"); Lazy.table(); LOG.add("-- Lazy.table() called --"); Lazy.table(); LOG.forEach(System.out::println); } }

alt.title: InitOrderDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.startup.l01.demo /** Prints the moment each initializer runs. Predict the order before you run it. */ private val log = mutableListOf<String>() private fun build(who: String): Map<String, String> { log += who // the expensive part would go here return mapOf("411111" to "Northwind Bank") } /** A companion's properties are static fields of Fees: built when Fees is initialized. */ class Fees { companion object { val table = build("Fees companion: table built with the outer class") fun version() = "fees-v1" } } /** A nested object is its own class, with its own initializer: the Kotlin holder idiom. */ object Bins { fun version() = "bins-v1" fun table() = Holder.table private object Holder { val table = build("Bins.Holder: table built") } } /** by lazy: built on the first get, under a lock by default (LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED). */ object Rates { fun version() = "rates-v1" val table by lazy { build("Rates lazy: table built") } } fun main() { log += "main starts" Fees.version() Bins.version() Rates.version() log += "-- all three versions read --" Bins.table() Rates.table log += "-- Bins.table() and Rates.table read --" log.forEach(::println) }

try.expect: Java prints main starts, Eager.<clinit> builds the table, Lazy.<clinit> (no table here), -- both versions read --, Lazy.Holder.<clinit> builds the table, -- Lazy.table() called --. Calling Eager.version() built a table nobody asked for. The second Lazy.table() prints nothing: a class is initialized once. In Kotlin, Fees.version() builds the companion's table, while Bins and Rates build theirs only after -- all three versions read --.

sections.h: Three clocks, and only one is what users see
sections.html:
There are three start-up numbers, and people mix them up.

The first is the JVM's own. -Xlog:startuptime prints the phases of creating the VM and ends with a line like Create VM, 0.0381310 secs. That is the JVM getting ready to run main. It says nothing about your code or your framework.

The second is the framework's log line. Quarkus prints started in 0.968s. Listening on: http://localhost:8080. That number comes from inside the process, and every framework starts its clock at a slightly different place.

The third is time to first request: from launching the process to the first successful response, measured from outside. This is the one that matters. A Kubernetes readiness probe, a load balancer and a user all see this clock and no other. It includes everything: the launcher, VM creation, class loading, framework start, and the first request itself, which loads more classes again (the HTTP handler path, JSON, your service code).

On a shared 4-vCPU Linux VM, the demo below printed this for a tiny JDK HttpServer app on JDK 21:

log      : [0.031s][info][startuptime] Create VM, 0.0301657 secs
log      : started in 0.103s. Listening on: http://127.0.0.1:45969
first 200: 179 ms after launch, measured outside (15 attempts)

30 ms, 103 ms and 179 ms. The gap between the last two is the launcher, process creation, and the first request's own class loading.

Even the first 200 is not the end. Early requests run in the interpreter or in C1-compiled code, and the C2 compiler only takes over hot methods after it has seen enough of them. So time to first request and time to peak throughput are different numbers too. You can feel this when a new pod joins under load: it answers, but slowly, for a while. The performance track's first lesson, "From bytecode to machine code", goes into the tiers.

try.title: Read all three clocks
steps: Read FirstRequestTimer. It picks a free port, starts the same class as a service in a second JVM, polls /hello every 2 ms from outside, and stops the clock at the first 200.
Run it with -Pargs=-Xlog:startuptime added to the command below. Note the three numbers.
Predict what -Pargs=-Xshare:off does to each clock, then run it.

code.title: FirstRequestTimer.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l01.demo; import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer; import java.io.IOException; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.net.ServerSocket; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpClient; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; /** * Launches a tiny HTTP service in a second JVM and reads three clocks: the JVM's own * "Create VM" line (pass -Xlog:startuptime), the service's "started in" line, and the time * to the first 200, measured from outside. Then it reads the service's RSS. */ public class FirstRequestTimer { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 1 && args[0].equals("--serve")) { serve(Integer.parseInt(args[1])); return; } int port; try (ServerSocket s = new ServerSocket(0, 1, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress())) { port = s.getLocalPort(); // a free port for the service } List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(List.of(args)); // e.g. -Xlog:startuptime, -Xshare:off cmd.addAll(List.of("-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), FirstRequestTimer.class.getName(), "--serve", Integer.toString(port))); // 1. warm up our own HTTP client (nothing listens yet), then start the clock and the service HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build(); HttpRequest hello = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + port + "/hello")).build(); try { client.send(hello, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()); } catch (IOException expected) { // refused: good, the client's own classes are loaded now } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); Process service = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); List<String> serviceLog = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().start(() -> service.inputReader().lines().forEach(serviceLog::add)); // 2. poll from outside every 2 ms until the first 200 int attempts = 0; long firstOk = -1; while (firstOk < 0 && System.nanoTime() - t0 < Duration.ofSeconds(8).toNanos()) { attempts++; try { if (client.send(hello, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).statusCode() == 200) { firstOk = System.nanoTime() - t0; } } catch (IOException notUpYet) { Thread.sleep(2); } } // 3. footprint of the whole process, as the OS sees it, and the JVM's own accounting String rss = rss(service.pid()); List<String> nmt = List.of(args).stream().anyMatch(a -> a.startsWith("-XX:NativeMemoryTracking")) ? nmt(service.pid()) : List.of(); service.destroy(); service.waitFor(); System.out.printf("JDK %s, flags %s%n", Runtime.version(), List.of(args)); serviceLog.stream().filter(l -> l.contains("Create VM") || l.contains("started in")) .forEach(l -> System.out.println(" log : " + l)); System.out.printf(" first 200: %d ms after launch, measured outside (%d attempts)%n", firstOk / 1_000_000, attempts); System.out.println(" RSS : " + rss); nmt.forEach(l -> System.out.println(" NMT : " + l)); } /** Asks the running service for its Native Memory Tracking summary (needs -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary). */ static List<String> nmt(long pid) throws Exception { String jcmd = Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "jcmd").toString(); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(jcmd, Long.toString(pid), "VM.native_memory", "summary", "scale=MB") .redirectErrorStream(true).start(); try (var lines = p.inputReader().lines()) { return lines.filter(l -> l.contains("Total:") || l.contains("Java Heap (")) .map(l -> l.replace("-", "").trim()).toList(); } } /** RSS from /proc on Linux, from ps elsewhere. Both count the whole process, not just the heap. */ static String rss(long pid) throws Exception { Path status = Path.of("/proc", Long.toString(pid), "status"); if (Files.exists(status)) { List<String> keep = Files.readAllLines(status).stream() .filter(l -> l.startsWith("VmRSS") || l.startsWith("RssAnon") || l.startsWith("RssFile")) .map(l -> l.replaceAll("\\s+", " ")) .toList(); return String.join(", ", keep); } Process ps = new ProcessBuilder("ps", "-o", "rss=", "-p", Long.toString(pid)).start(); return new String(ps.getInputStream().readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8).trim() + " kB (ps)"; } /** The service: one endpoint, and a Quarkus-style "started in" line, from the JVM's uptime. */ static void serve(int port) throws Exception { HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port), 0); server.createContext("/hello", exchange -> { byte[] body = "{\"status\":\"AUTHORIZED\",\"amountMinor\":1250}".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8); exchange.getResponseHeaders().add("Content-Type", "application/json"); exchange.sendResponseHeaders(200, body.length); exchange.getResponseBody().write(body); exchange.close(); }); server.start(); long uptimeMs = ManagementFactory.getRuntimeMXBean().getUptime(); // since the JVM started System.out.printf("started in %.3fs. Listening on: http://127.0.0.1:%d%n", uptimeMs / 1000.0, port); } }

Then it reads the service's RSS. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.size > 1 && args[0] == "--serve") { serve(args[1].toInt()) return } val port = ServerSocket(0, 1, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress()).use { it.localPort } val cmd = buildList { add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()) addAll(args) // e.g. -Xlog:startuptime, -Xshare:off addAll(listOf("-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.startup.l01.demo.FirstRequestTimerKt", "--serve", port.toString())) } // 1. warm up our own HTTP client (nothing listens yet), then start the clock and the service val client = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build() val hello = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:$port/hello")).build() try { client.send(hello, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()) } catch (expected: IOException) { // refused: good, the client's own classes are loaded now } val t0 = System.nanoTime() val service = ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start() val serviceLog = CopyOnWriteArrayList<String>() thread(isDaemon = true) { service.inputReader().lines().forEach(serviceLog::add) } // 2. poll from outside every 2 ms until the first 200 var attempts = 0 var firstOk = -1L while (firstOk < 0 && System.nanoTime() - sections.h: Footprint is RSS, and the heap is only part of it
sections.html:
The same demo also reads the service's memory, and the numbers disagree by a factor of five.

RSS      : VmRSS: 53456 kB, RssAnon: 28824 kB, RssFile: 24632 kB
NMT      : Total: reserved=4901MB, committed=290MB
NMT      : Java Heap (reserved=3420MB, committed=216MB)

Native Memory Tracking (NMT) is the JVM's own accounting. It says the JVM has committed 290 MB, 216 MB of it for the heap. The operating system says the process has 53 MB resident (RSS). Both are right. Committed memory is memory the JVM has asked the OS for. A page only becomes resident when someone touches it, and a fresh heap is mostly untouched pages.

RSS is the number the container limit cares about. It is much more than the heap. It counts touched heap pages, metaspace and the class space, the JIT's code cache, GC data structures, thread stacks, the mapped CDS archive, the JDK's modules file, libjvm.so, direct buffers and malloc arenas. RssAnon is memory the process created for itself. RssFile is file-backed pages, such as the JDK's modules file and libjvm.so, and processes that map the same file can share them. For shared pages, Pss in /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup splits each one between the processes that map it.

Measure it like this:

ps -o pid,rss,args -p <pid>                 # RSS in kB, Linux and macOS
grep -E 'VmRSS|RssAnon|RssFile' /proc/<pid>/status
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary         # only if started with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary

Don't use docker stats. The Quarkus guide on measuring performance says so in capitals: it "only measures a subset of the in-use resident pages", while a container is killed "based on its full RSS memory usage". It recommends ps -e -o pid,rss,args or docker top <id> -o pid,rss,args instead.

One more trap: heap usage from your metrics dashboard is not footprint either. It leaves out everything in the list above, and it counts live objects, not the heap pages the GC has already touched.

try.title: Committed is not resident
steps: Run FirstRequestTimer again with -Pargs=-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary. The demo asks the running service for its NMT summary with jcmd before it stops it.
Compare the Total: committed line with VmRSS. Which one would a 512 MiB container limit compare against?
On Linux, run cat /proc/self/status | grep Rss in a shell to see the same fields for cat itself.

Then it reads the service's RSS. */ public class FirstRequestTimer { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 1 && args[0].equals("--serve")) { serve(Integer.parseInt(args[1])); return; } int port; try (ServerSocket s = new ServerSocket(0, 1, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress())) { port = s.getLocalPort(); // a free port for the service } List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(List.of(args)); // e.g. -Xlog:startuptime, -Xshare:off cmd.addAll(List.of("-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), FirstRequestTimer.class.getName(), "--serve", Integer.toString(port))); // 1. warm up our own HTTP client (nothing listens yet), then start the clock and the service HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build(); HttpRequest hello = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + port + "/hello")).build(); try { client.send(hello, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()); } catch (IOException expected) { // refused: good, the client's own classes are loaded now } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); Process service = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); List<String> serviceLog = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().start(() -> service.inputReader().lines().forEach(serviceLog::add)); // 2. poll from outside every 2 ms until the first 200 int attempts = 0; long firstOk = -1; while (firstOk < 0 && System.nanoTime() - t0 < Duration.ofSeconds(8).toNanos()) { attempts++; try { if (client.send(hello, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).statusCode() == 200) { firstOk = System.nanoTime() - t0; } } catch (IOException notUpYet) { Thread.sleep(2); } } // 3. footprint of the whole process, as the OS sees it, and the JVM's own accounting String rss = rss(service.pid()); List<String> nmt = List.of(args).stream().anyMatch(a -> a.startsWith("-XX:NativeMemoryTracking")) ? nmt(service.pid()) : List.of(); service.destroy(); service.waitFor(); System.out.printf("JDK %s, flags %s%n", Runtime.version(), List.of(args)); serviceLog.stream().filter(l -> l.contains("Create VM") || l.contains("started in")) .forEach(l -> System.out.println(" log : " + l)); System.out.printf(" first 200: %d ms after launch, measured outside (%d attempts)%n", firstOk / 1_000_000, attempts); System.out.println(" RSS : " + rss); nmt.forEach(l -> System.out.println(" NMT : " + l)); } /** Asks the running service for its Native Memory Tracking summary (needs -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary). */ static List<String> nmt(long pid) throws Exception { String jcmd = Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "jcmd").toString(); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(jcmd, Long.toString(pid), "VM.native_memory", "summary", "scale=MB") .redirectErrorStream(true).start(); try (var lines = p.inputReader().lines()) { return lines.filter(l -> l.contains("Total:") || l.contains("Java Heap (")) .map(l -> l.replace("-", "").trim()).toList(); } } /** RSS from /proc on Linux, from ps elsewhere. Both count the whole process, not just the heap. */ static String rss(long pid) throws Exception { Path status = Path.of("/proc", Long.toString(pid), "status"); if (Files.exists(status)) { List<String> keep = Files.readAllLines(status).stream() .filter(l -> l.startsWith("VmRSS") || l.startsWith("RssAnon") || l.startsWith("RssFile")) .map(l -> l.replaceAll("\\s+", " ")) .toList(); return String.join(", ", keep); } Process ps = new ProcessBuilder("ps", "-o", "rss=", "-p", Long.toString(pid)).start(); return new String(ps.getInputStream().readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8).trim() + " kB (ps)"; } /** The service: one endpoint, and a Quarkus-style "started in" line, from the JVM's uptime. */ static void serve(int port) throws Exception { HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port), 0); server.createContext("/hello", exchange -> { byte[] body = "{\"status\":\"AUTHORIZED\",\"amountMinor\":1250}".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8); exchange.getResponseHeaders().add("Content-Type", "application/json"); exchange.sendResponseHeaders(200, body.length); exchange.getResponseBody().write(body); exchange.close(); }); server.start(); long uptimeMs = ManagementFactory.getRuntimeMXBean().getUptime(); // since the JVM started System.out.printf("started in %.3fs. Listening on: http://127.0.0.1:%d%n", uptimeMs / 1000.0, port); } }

try.expect: Here NMT reported committed=290MB with Java Heap ... committed=216MB, while VmRSS was about 53,000 kB. The JVM has reserved and committed far more than it has touched. The container limit counts resident memory, so RSS is the number to watch. On macOS the demo prints the ps value instead of the /proc breakdown.

refs.title: Quarkus: Measuring performance (RSS, not docker stats)

analogy: Think of a shop that throws its stock away every night. Each morning someone unpacks every box, checks each item against the invoice, and puts it on a shelf before the first customer comes in. The lights going on is Create VM. The "open" sign is the framework's started in line. The first customer leaving with a receipt is the first 200, and that is the only moment the street cares about. A holder class is a box you leave sealed in the back until somebody asks for what is in it. The analogy breaks in one place: a real shop would keep its shelves stocked overnight. The JVM keeps nothing between runs unless you give it an archive, which is lesson 2.
world: Your Quarkus payment service runs as pods behind a readiness probe. Every scale-out under load, every rolling deploy and every @QuarkusIntegrationTest JVM pays the whole start-up again, and a new pod is slowest at the moment traffic is highest. Look for static work that every start pays for: a BIN or FX rate table built in a companion object, a Kafka schema registry client created in a static field, a big JSON mapping config parsed in <clinit>. Measure from outside: launch the pod and poll /q/health/ready until it answers 200, like the lab's probe does. For memory, read ps -o rss or /proc/<pid>/status inside the container, never docker stats and never just the heap from your metrics dashboard.
mistake: The common mistake is reading the wrong number and tuning against it. A team sees started in 0.9s in the Quarkus log and 180 MiB in docker stats and calls it done, while the readiness probe needs 2.5 s to see a 200 and the container's RSS is close to its limit. The framework's clock starts late and stops early, and docker stats counts only part of the resident pages. Measure time to first request from outside the process, read RSS from ps or /proc, and keep NMT for the question of where inside the JVM the memory went.

compare.title: A lazy table in Java and in Kotlin

java.title: IssuerDirectory.java
java.html: public final class IssuerDirectory { // eager: built in IssuerDirectory.<clinit>, on the first use of the class private static final Map<String, String> ALIASES = loadAliases(); // lazy: built in Holder.<clinit>, on the first read of Holder.BINS private static final class Holder { static final Map<String, String> BINS = loadBins(); } public static String version() { return "dir-v7"; } public static String issuerOf(String pan) { return Holder.BINS.get(pan.substring(0, 6)); } }

kotlin.title: IssuerDirectory.kt
kotlin.html: object IssuerDirectory { // eager: built in IssuerDirectory.<clinit>, on the first use of the object private val aliases = loadAliases() // lazy: Holder is its own class with its own <clinit> private object Holder { val bins = loadBins() } // also lazy, with a visible lock (LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED by default) val rates by lazy { loadRates() } fun version() = "dir-v7" fun issuerOf(pan: String) = Holder.bins[pan.take(6)] }

compare.note: Both compile to the same JVM mechanism: a static field filled in a class initializer, which runs once, on first active use, under the JVM's class-initialization lock. What differs is where Kotlin puts the fields. Properties of an object live in the object's class. Properties of a companion object live as static fields of the outer class, so touching the outer class at all builds them. A private nested object is the exact twin of Java's holder. by lazy is a library feature, not a JVM one: it allocates a Lazy object and takes a lock on first access, which costs a little but works for instance properties too, where the holder idiom cannot help.

worked.title: Find and fix a companion object that builds on start-up

steps.say: A readiness check calls FxRates.source() to report where the rates came from. Start-up got 400 ms slower after this class was added. Here it is, with the Java equivalent next to it.
steps.code: class FxRates { companion object { private val rates: Map<String, Double> = loadRatesFile() // 400 ms fun source() = "ecb-daily" fun rate(currency: String) = rates.getValue(currency) } }

alt.html: public final class FxRates { private static final Map<String, Double> RATES = loadRatesFile(); // 400 ms public static String source() { return "ecb-daily"; } public static double rate(String currency) { return RATES.get(currency); } }

steps.say: Check where the field lives with javap -p on the compiled class. The rates field sits on FxRates, not on the companion, and FxRates's static initializer fills it. So source() initializes FxRates, and that loads the file.
Give the rates their own class. The readiness check now touches only FxRates. The first call to rate initializes Holder and pays the 400 ms once.
steps.code: object FxRates { fun source() = "ecb-daily" fun rate(currency: String) = Holder.rates.getValue(currency) // 1. its own class, so its own initializer private object Holder { val rates: Map<String, Double> = loadRatesFile() } }

alt.html: public final class FxRates { public static String source() { return "ecb-daily"; } public static double rate(String currency) { return Holder.RATES.get(currency); } // 1. its own class, so its own initializer private static final class Holder { static final Map<String, Double> RATES = loadRatesFile(); } }

$ java -Xlog:class+load -jar app.jar | grep FxRates
[info][class,load] com.acme.fx.FxRates source: file:/srv/app.jar
... (readiness check passes, first payment arrives) ...
[info][class,load] com.acme.fx.FxRates$Holder source: file:/srv/app.jar

lab.title: Take a table off the start-up path, and build a readiness probe
steps: Run the tests once. Five of the nine fail: version() does not build the table, and all four probe tests.
Fix BinTable with the holder idiom. Move TABLE into a private static final class Holder and read Holder.TABLE in issuerOf. Keep calling build().

Write FirstRequestProbe.await. Build one HttpRequest with a short timeout. Loop up to maxAttempts: send it, record the status as a string, and stop at 200. Catch java.net.ConnectException and record "refused". Sleep pause between attempts.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then read BinTableTest: each test gets a FreshLoader, so each one sees a class nobody has initialized yet.
hints: Why does the test need a fresh class loader? A class is initialized once per loader. If every test used the normal loader, the first test to call issuerOf would build the table and every later test would see it already built.
client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.discarding()) returns a response whose statusCode() you need. Nothing else of the body matters.
ConnectException extends IOException, so catch it first. Treat other IOExceptions (a reset while the server starts) as a failed attempt too.
lab.done: All nine tests in BinTableTest and FirstRequestProbeTest pass.

drill.title: Write the holder idiom from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a class CountryRules with static String version() that returns "rules-3" and static String regionOf(String country) that reads from a map built by an expensive load() method. version() must never call load(), and load() must run once even under concurrent first calls, with no synchronized in your code. Then write the Kotlin version with an object.

answer.html: public final class CountryRules { private static final class Holder { // runs once, on the first read of Holder.RULES, under the JVM's init lock static final Map<String, String> RULES = load(); } public static String version() { return "rules-3"; } public static String regionOf(String country) { return Holder.RULES.getOrDefault(country, "unknown"); } private static Map<String, String> load() { return Map.of("DE", "EU", "FR", "EU", "US", "NA"); // imagine a big file } }

alt.html: object CountryRules { fun version() = "rules-3" fun regionOf(country: String) = Holder.rules[country] ?: "unknown" // a nested object is its own class: initialized on first use, once private object Holder { val rules: Map<String, String> = load() } private fun load() = mapOf("DE" to "EU", "FR" to "EU", "US" to "NA") // imagine a big file }

recap: A start-up repeats the same work every launch: load, parse and verify about 1,500 classes for a 300-class app, run static initializers, interpret until the JIT has profiles, and run the framework's own start-up.
-Xlog:class+load shows each class and its source: shared objects file (CDS archive), jrt:/ (parsed from the JDK), file: (your classpath), or a defining class for hidden classes.
A class's <clinit> runs on first active use. A Kotlin companion's properties are static fields of the outer class; a nested object or a Java holder class is lazy.
Three clocks: Create VM from -Xlog:startuptime, the framework's started in, and time to first request from outside. Only the last is what a probe or user sees.
Footprint is the whole process's RSS. NMT committed memory includes untouched pages, and docker stats sees only part of the resident set.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our service starts in 0.9 seconds and uses 180 MiB. I read it in the Quarkus log and in docker stats." Explain what each number leaves out and what you would measure instead.
explain.answer: The 0.9 seconds is the framework's own clock, taken inside the process. It starts after the launcher and JVM creation, and it stops before the first request, which loads more classes and runs in the interpreter. The readiness probe and the users see the time from launch to the first 200, so I'd poll the readiness endpoint from outside and time that. The 180 MiB from docker stats covers only part of the resident pages. The container is killed on its full RSS, which includes metaspace, the code cache, thread stacks, the mapped archive and the touched heap. I'd read RSS with ps -o rss or /proc/<pid>/status, and use NMT only to see which part of the JVM the memory went to.

deeper.html:
Loading is lazy, but not as lazy as the rule above suggests. Two things load classes you never called.

The first is the verifier. To check that a method is type-safe, it sometimes needs to know whether one class is a subtype of another, for example when two branches produce different classes that meet at the same variable. To answer that, it loads both classes. A prototype of lesson 2's lab hit this: a test fixture whose static initializer read a field of its outer class pulled in the outer class, and verifying that class pulled in more. That is why the lab compares the exact set of classes your loader defined, taken from a run of the reference answer, and never a count of all loaded classes, which changes from one JDK build to the next.

The second is the framework. Annotation scanning reads class files to find @Path or @ApplicationScoped, and reflection-driven dependency injection loads every bean class at start-up. This is the work Quarkus moves to build time. At build time it indexes the classes (Jandex), decides the wiring and generates plain bytecode that does it, so at run time there is no scanning and much less reflection. Its extension guide puts it as registering classes "at build time and generating code that registers them at static-init time instead of relying on reflection". Spring's AOT mode makes a similar move with a different design.

If you want to see where a large app spends its start-up, -Xlog:class+load piped through sed -E 's/.*source: //' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head gives the same histogram as the demo, and the JFR jdk.ClassLoad event, which is off by default, records a stack trace for each load once you enable it. Measure first, then pick a fix from lessons 2 to 4.
